\text{For symmetric cutoffs at the original pole, the transformed cutoff ratio tends to one.}
\text{In the upper piece use }u=1/t\text{; combine both pieces on }(0,1).

statement: \textnormal{For }I=\int_0^\infty\frac{x^{0}}{1-x^{3}}\,\mathrm{d}x\textnormal{, choose the pair (ordinary integral, Cauchy principal value at }x=1\textnormal{).}

analyticCertificate: Near x=1 the integrand has a nonzero simple-pole residue, so the two one-sided improper integrals diverge.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Use a polynomial whose sign is orthogonal to every polynomial of smaller degree. Define the second-kind Chebyshev polynomials by their recurrence.}
U_0(x)=1,\quad U_1(x)=2x,\quad U_{j+1}(x)=2xU_j(x)-U_{j-1}(x),\quad U_j(\cos t)=\frac{\sin((j+1)t)}{\sin t}.

\textnormal{The leading coefficient of U is two to its degree, so q is monic. Under x equal to cosine t, every lower-degree monomial times the Jacobian is a finite linear combination of sine modes of frequency at most n.}

\textnormal{Indeed, the square-wave sign has only odd multiples of frequency n plus one in its sine expansion; sine orthogonality eliminates every lower frequency. Equivalently, integrating separately on its finitely many sign intervals gives the same identities.}
\textnormal{The difference between any monic p and q has degree below n. The sign moment identities therefore give a universal lower bound.}

\textnormal{Equality requires p to have the sign of U almost everywhere. At every simple interior zero of U its sign changes, so continuity forces a zero of p there. There are n such distinct roots; monicity forces p to equal q.}
\textnormal{The displayed next-to-leading coefficient follows by substituting the leading two coefficients into the recurrence.}
statement: \textnormal{Among real monic polynomials p of the displayed degree, let M be the minimum integral below. Its minimizing polynomial is unique; let c be its coefficient of the indicated power. Find the ordered pair.}\quad\deg p=5,\qquad M=\min_p\int_{-1}^{1}|p(x)|\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad c=[x^{3}]p(x),\qquad(M,c)=?

analyticCertificate: The sign of sin((n+1)t) has its usual L2 sine expansion with frequencies (2r+1)(n+1). Multiplication by the finite sine polynomial sin(t)cos(t)^j permits orthogonality term by term by L2 convergence, not an unjustified pointwise boundary interchange. The finitely many roots cos(k*pi/(n+1)),1<=k<=n, are simple and interior. The nonnegative defect |p|-p*sigma has zero integral only if it vanishes almost everywhere; continuity on each sign interval then forces the required alternating signs. Consequently all n interior roots belong to p, proving uniqueness. The independent verifier checks every finite sign moment directly in the cyclotomic field, without using the Fourier argument.

\textnormal{The leading coefficient of U is two to its degree, so q is monic. Under x equal to cosine t, every lower-degree monomial times the Jacobian is a finite linear combination of sine modes of frequency at most n.}

\textnormal{Indeed, the square-wave sign has only odd multiples of frequency n plus one in its sine expansion; sine orthogonality eliminates every lower frequency. Equivalently, integrating separately on its finitely many sign intervals gives the same identities.}
\textnormal{The difference between any monic p and q has degree below n. The sign moment identities therefore give a universal lower bound.}

\textnormal{Equality requires p to have the sign of U almost everywhere. At every simple interior zero of U its sign changes, so continuity forces a zero of p there. There are n such distinct roots; monicity forces p to equal q.}
\textnormal{The displayed next-to-leading coefficient follows by substituting the leading two coefficients into the recurrence.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The phase is nonnegative and vanishes only at the interior point zero and the endpoint one. Their orders determine different localization scales.}

\textnormal{Near zero put x equal to n to the power minus one over two p times u. Near one put one minus x equal to n to the power minus one over two q times v. The logarithmic tilt is asymptotically constant on each rescaled neighborhood.}
n^{\tau x}=\exp(\tau x\ln n),\qquad n^{-1/(2p)}\ln n\to0,\quad n^{-1/(2q)}\ln n\to0.
\textnormal{Let J zero and J one denote the masses in fixed small neighborhoods of zero and one, respectively.}
\textnormal{Away from both neighborhoods the phase has a positive minimum, so the exponential decay defeats every fixed power from the tilt.}

\textnormal{For the local dominated limits, the phase bounds give an exponential of a negative even power. The residual tilted linear term has a coefficient tending to zero, and can be absorbed into half that negative power plus a fixed constant. This supplies an integrable bound.}
\textnormal{The factor x in the numerator tends to zero at the first well and one at the second. It is bounded, so the same domination justifies those weighted limits.}
\textnormal{The two powers match. The limiting first moment is the endpoint mass divided by the sum of both local masses.}
statement: V(x)=x^{2} \left(1 - x\right)^{4},\qquad w_n(x)=n^{(- \frac{1}{4})x}e^{-nV(x)}\quad(-1\le x\le1,\ n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}).\quad \textnormal{Find the limit of the normalized first moment.}\quad\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\int_{-1}^{1}xw_n(x)\,\mathrm{d}x}{\int_{-1}^{1}w_n(x)\,\mathrm{d}x}.\qquad\Gamma(a)=\int_0^\infty t^{a-1}e^{-t}\,\mathrm{d}t\quad(a>0).

analyticCertificate: Choose disjoint fixed neighborhoods of0 and1 inside[-1,1]. The polynomial has no other zeros, so its minimum on the remaining compact set is positive. Near each well its ratio to the leading even power tends to1 and stays bounded below by a positive constant. After rescaling, the tilt remainder is b_n times the local variable with b_n tending to0. For sufficiently large n, |b_n u| is at most half the leading negative even power plus a uniform finite constant, giving a global integrable rescaled majorant. The interior neighborhood expands to the whole real line; the endpoint neighborhood expands only to the positive half-line. Gamma substitution and recurrence evaluate the two constants. Dominated convergence also applies with the bounded multiplier x. Comparing the exact rational relative exponent proves the three requested regimes.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Let I denote the requested principal value and a the displayed pole. Separate the nonsingular polynomial part from the singular arcsine kernel.}
\textnormal{The second term integrates directly: its odd part vanishes, while the arcsine mass is pi. It remains to show that the first term has zero principal value.}
\textnormal{Use x equal to cosine theta, then the tangent of half theta. The pole is an interior positive point in the new variable.}
\textnormal{A chosen real antiderivative on each side of the pole has the following logarithmic form and vanishes at both external endpoints.}

\textnormal{The original equal x cutoffs need not be equal in t. Their distances from b nevertheless have ratio tending to one, because the inverse substitution has a finite nonzero derivative at the pole. The two logarithmic divergences therefore cancel with no residual constant.}
statement: \textnormal{Evaluate the Cauchy principal value defined by the displayed equal-distance cutoffs around the interior pole. analyticCertificate: The semicircle density is continuous at the interior pole, and its first derivative is bounded near that point. Subtracting its value at the pole leaves a locally bounded quotient, which independently ensures the symmetric principal value exists. At the two external endpoints both the original square-root kernel and the separated arcsine terms are integrable. The cosine and half-angle substitutions are applied first with the exact transformed cutoffs, not with an assumed symmetric new cutoff. The inverse map has nonzero derivative at the pole, so the two new distances have ratio one asymptotically. In the displayed logarithmic primitive, the regular numerators have the same limit; hence the cutoff difference vanishes. This proves the zero arcsine principal value and the stated result.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The rule is exact on constants and linear functions, so only the integral remainder in Taylor expansion contributes. Define the interior node and the three weights.}
\textnormal{Interchange the continuous triangular integral and collect the quadrature evaluations. The resulting kernel is piecewise quadratic.}
\textnormal{The kernel is negative near both endpoints and positive in the middle. Its two interior zeros determine the exact absolute integral.}

\textnormal{Choose continuous second derivatives bounded by one that agree with the kernel sign outside shrinking neighborhoods of the two zeros. Integrating them twice gives admissible functions; dominated convergence makes their errors tend to this bound.}

\textnormal{Equality would require the second derivative to equal the kernel sign almost everywhere, up to one common sign. Continuity would then force opposite one-sided values at each sign-changing zero. This is impossible, so the supremum is not attained.}
statement: \textnormal{For real twice continuously differentiable f on the unit interval with the displayed derivative bound, define the quadrature error E. Find the ordered pair consisting of its sharp supremum C and the answer yes or no to whether an admissible f attains it.}\quad |f\prime\prime(x)|\le1\quad(0\le x\le1),\qquad E(f)=\int_0^1f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x-\left(\frac{1}{12}f(0)+\frac{5}{8}f(\frac{1}{3})+\frac{7}{24}f(1)\right),\qquad C=\sup_f|E(f)|.

analyticCertificate: Taylor integral remainder holds for every admitted C2 function. Fubini is valid because its integrand is continuous on a compact triangle. \textnormal{A positive candidate is obtained with cosine coefficient one and sine coefficient k. It satisfies both boundary conditions and has no zero on the interval.}
\textnormal{Now prove the bound for every admissible function, without assuming that the formal variational calculation found the minimum. Define the logarithmic derivative v and complete a square.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The nonconvex cost has two zero wells. The best lower bound must allow mixtures of those wells rather than apply Jensen directly to the quartic.}
\textnormal{Nonnegativity gives a lower bound of zero. A measurable mixture with the prescribed mean takes the two well values in the following proportions.}

\textnormal{For a strictly mixed mean, put the single interior transition at t zero as follows. Use linear ramps from minus two to minus one on the first interval, from minus one to one across the middle interval, and from one to two on the last interval. On the remaining intervals keep the neighboring well value.}

\textnormal{Attaining zero cost would force the continuous function to take only the two well values everywhere. It could not have either of the prescribed endpoint values; by continuity an endpoint neighborhood already has positive cost.}
\textnormal{Thus the lower bound is an infimum reached by a sequence, and is not attained by any admissible continuous function.}
statement: \textnormal{Let f range over continuous real functions satisfying the displayed range, endpoint values and mean. Find the ordered pair consisting of the infimum of J and the answer yes or no to whether it is attained.}\quad -2\le f(x)\le2\quad(0\le x\le1),\quad f(0)=-2,\quad f(1)=2,\quad\int_0^1f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=0,\qquad J(f)=\int_0^1(f(x)^2-1)^2\,\mathrm{d}x.

analyticCertificate: For means inside the two wells, nonnegativity supplies the lower bound and a two-phase mixture supplies its measurable value. One can approximate that mixture by a continuous piecewise linear function on shrinking transition intervals while enforcing the mean exactly: for a strictly mixed mean adjust a phase length, and for the pure mean one adjust the middle level slightly above or below the well. These adjustments tend to zero and stay inside[-2,2] for small transition lengths; the cost is bounded on the allowed range, so shrinking transitions have vanishing cost. For means above one, the exact tangent-defect factorization gives a global lower bound without an invalid Jensen invocation on the quartic. The explicitly displayed constant-middle recovery function has exact mean and remains inside the allowed range for the stated delta interval; dominated convergence gives its cost limit. Continuous endpoint incompatibility prevents zero cost in the mixed regime, while strict supporting-line equality forces a forbidden constant in the outer regime.
